To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) in an online labor setting, codes of conduct and social norms are ineffective in deterring dishonest reporting, (2) monitoring with economic penalties is effective in deterring dishonest behavior, (3) the effect of monitoring with penalties is most pronounced among workers who are most likely to report dishonestly, and (4) monitoring without penalties is not effective in deterring unethical reporting.

(1) in online labor markets where workers are anonymous and transient, monitoring with economic sanctions is effective in promoting honest reporting, (2) this effect is particularly strong among workers who rate high on a personality trait associated with dishonest reporting, and (3) codes of conduct and social norms are ineffective in this setting.

codes of conduct and penalties without monitoring are ineffective in online labor markets; monitoring without penalties is effective in online labor markets for workers who rate low in Machiavelianism, and monitoring with penalties is effective in all online labor markets.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the problem of dishonest reporting in online labor markets and the effectiveness of codes of conduct, economic monitoring, and economic penalties in addressing this issue.
the issue of ethical behavior in the context of online labor markets.
the question of how to promote honest reporting in online labor markets.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
codes of conduct and social norms can be effective tools to deter unethical behavior in online labor markets.

the results show that monitoring with economic penalties is an effective method for increasing reporting honesty in an experimental online labor market, and that this effect is strongest for those who are most likely to engage in dishonest behavior.
the results of this study show that the use of economic penalties is an effective method of promoting honest reporting in online labor markets.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
codes of conduct, without monitoring or penalties, are not effective in promoting honest reporting in an experimental setting.
the use of codes of conduct and social norms are not enough to promote ethical behavior in an online setting; rather, economic penalties are required.
codes of conduct and other non-economic incentives are not effective in promoting honest reporting in online labor markets.
The main takeaway from our work is that
online labor markets are unique settings that require different methods for promoting ethical behavior than those that have been shown effective in other settings.
companies can use monitoring with economic penalties as an effective means of deterring unethical behavior in online settings.
companies and researchers should be cautious when using online labor markets to gather data, and should consider using monitoring with penalties to promote honest reporting.
